hello.note: Literally "may you live long", said with palms pressed together, to anyone, at any time. Also goodbye. Friends just say හලෝ (HA-loh)

how-are-you.note: Literally "how?", the everyday way to ask. Among friends add ඉතින් (I-tin): කොහොමද ඉතින්?

im-well.note: The nd is said with a little n before the d. The same for a man or a woman

good-morning.note: Formal. Most people simply say ආයුබෝවන්, or good morning in English

good-night.note: Formal. Good night in English is common too

goodbye.note: Literally "I'll go and come back", the usual goodbye. ආයුබෝවන් works too

please.note: Rather formal. Spoken Sinhala is polite through the verb: ... දෙන්න (DEN-na), please give

thank-you.note: Thank you very much is ගොඩක් ස්තූතියි (GO-dak STOO-ti-yi)

yes.note: A sideways wobble of the head often means yes, or OK

no.note: To turn down something offered: එපා, ස්තූතියි (E-paa, STOO-ti-yi), no, thank you

excuse-me.note: Sorry, and excuse me to get someone's attention

my-name.note: No verb is needed: literally "my name, ...". The audio uses Peter as the example name

your-name.note: ඔයා (O-yaa) is the friendly you, fine with people your age. To an older person, use their title instead, such as මහත්තයා (MA-hat-ta-yaa), sir

where-from.note: Answer මම ... ඉඳලා (MA-ma ... IN-da-laa), I'm from...

dont-understand.note: Literally "to me it doesn't come clear", the same for a man or a woman

speak-english.note: English is widely spoken in Colombo, in hotels, and wherever there are visitors

eight.note: The t here is said with the tongue curled back, unlike the t of හත (HA-ta), seven

thousand.note: Prices are in rupees, රුපියල් (RU-pi-yal), written Rs.

hundred-thousand.note: A lakh, as in India: big numbers are often counted in lakhs

million.note: Also ten lakhs, දස ලක්ෂය (DA-sa LAK-sha-ya)

how-much.note: Point at the thing, or say මේක කීයද? (MAY-ka KEE-ya-da), how much is this?

would-like.note: Literally "to me ... is needed", the usual way to ask, the same for a man or a woman. The audio uses තේ එකක් (TAY e-kak), a tea

i-want.note: Literally "please give ...", a polite request. The audio uses මේක (MAY-ka), this one

do-you-have.note: Literally "is there ...?" The audio uses වතුර (WA-tu-ra), water

ill-take-it.note: The same for a man or a woman

too-expensive.note: Literally "the price is a little much", a gentle way to start bargaining

discount.note: Bargaining is normal at markets and with tuk-tuks, not in shops with fixed prices. Agree a tuk-tuk fare before you set off, or use the PickMe or Uber app

card.note: Literally "can I pay by card?" Hotels and bigger shops take cards; carry cash for the rest

reservation.note: Booking, from English, is the usual word

breakfast.note: Try a Sri Lankan breakfast: hoppers, string hoppers, and coconut sambol

taxi.text: මට ටැක්සියක් කතා කරලා දෙන්න පුළුවන්ද?
taxi.say: MA-ta TAEK-si-yak KA-taa ka-ra-laa DEN-na PU-lu-wan-da
taxi.note: Literally "can you call a taxi for me?" Tuk-tuks are everywhere; PickMe and Uber work in the cities

train.note: Signs say දුම්රිය (DUM-ri-ya). The hill-country line from Kandy to Ella is one of the world's great train rides: book ahead

bus.note: එක (e-ka), one, after an English word makes it "the bus"

airport.note: The international airport is at Katunayake, about an hour north of Colombo. Airport in English is understood everywhere

bus-station.note: In speech, people usually say බස් ස්ටෑන්ඩ් එක (BAS STAEND e-ka), the bus stand

train-station.note: In speech, people often say ස්ටේෂන් එක (STAY-shan e-ka), the station

which-train.note: Literally "the ... train is which one?" The audio uses මහනුවර (MA-ha-nu-wa-ra), Kandy

buy-ticket.note: Literally "where do I get the ticket?"

two-tickets.note: Add ට (ta), to, to the place. The audio uses Kandy: මහනුවරට (MA-ha-nu-wa-ra-ta)

trip-length.note: Literally "to go to ..., how much time does it take?" The audio uses Kandy

allergic.note: Add the food, with ට (ta): රටකජු (RA-ta-ka-ju) peanuts, කජු (KA-ju) cashews, බිත්තර (BIT-ta-ra) eggs, ඉස්සෝ (IS-soh) prawns. The audio uses peanuts

love-dish.note: Literally "I'm very fond of this food"

table-for-two.note: For more people: තුන් දෙනෙකුට (TUN de-ne-ku-ta), 3, or හතර දෙනෙකුට (HA-ta-ra de-ne-ku-ta), 4

recommend.note: Literally "what's good?", the natural way to ask. Rice and curry is the national meal

beer.note: Lion is the local beer. No alcohol is sold on Poya days, the monthly full-moon holidays

tea.note: Ceylon tea, usually served sweet with milk: කිරි තේ (KI-ri TAY). Plain tea is ප්ලේන් ටී (PLAYN TEE)

sugar.note: Tea comes sweet. Without sugar is සීනි නැතුව (SEE-ni NAE-tu-wa)

hot.note: Hot to the touch, or a hot day. Spicy is සැරයි (SAE-ra-yi), and much Sri Lankan food is

cold.note: A cold drink is සීතල බීමක් (SEE-ta-la BEE-mak)

cheers.note: The English word is the usual toast

bill.note: Literally "please give the bill". A 10% service charge is often included

need-doctor.note: The same for a man or a woman. For an ambulance, call 1990, the free Suwa Seriya service

pharmacy.note: Signs may say ඖෂධ ශාලාව (OW-sha-da SHAA-laa-wa)
